summary.text: The van der Waals force is a distance-dependent interaction between atoms or molecules, and it is one kind of intermolecular force.
It does not come from a chemical electronic bond, so it is comparatively weak, and it quickly vanishes at longer distances between molecules.
It is usually described as a mix of London dispersion, Debye and Keesom forces, and it underlies properties of organic compounds such as their solubility.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: Dutch physicist Johannes Diderik van der Waals

facts.label: Three components
facts.value: London dispersion, Debye and Keesom forces

facts.label: Distance between atoms
facts.value: 0.3 to 0.5 nm at equilibrium for individual atoms

items.prompt: Two neighbouring molecules are slowly pulled much farther apart. What happens to the pull between them?

options.label: It stays about the same, since no bond is involved
It grows, since more room lets it act more freely
It quickly fades toward nothing at longer distances
It turns into a push once they are far apart

items.explain: The van der Waals force quickly vanishes at longer distances between interacting molecules.

items.prompt: Two atoms are pushed closer and closer together with no other force present. Past a certain distance, the pull turns into a push. What causes this?

options.label: The nuclei of the two atoms begin to fuse into one
The electron clouds of the two atoms repel each other
The atoms start a covalent bond that pushes back
The attraction runs out of strength at that distance

items.explain: The force becomes repulsive at the contact distance because of the mutual repulsion between the atoms' electron clouds.

items.prompt: A chemist compares the pairwise pull between small hydrogen atoms in H₂ with the pull between large xenon atoms. Which is stronger, and why?

options.label: Hydrogen, because smaller atoms sit closer together
They are equal, since both are neutral gases
Hydrogen, because it has the fewest electrons to repel
Xenon, because its larger atoms are more polarizable

items.explain: The strength increases with the polarizability of the atoms; the xenon interaction is up to 40 times stronger than in H₂.

items.prompt: Two atoms carry no net charge and form no chemical bond, yet they pull on each other. What is behind the pull?

options.label: Electron density briefly shifts to one side, leaving a temporary charge
A permanent positive charge hides inside every neutral atom
The two atoms briefly share an electron pair
The nuclei attract each other directly through empty space

items.explain: A transient shift in electron density generates a transient charge that a nearby atom can be attracted to or repelled by.

items.prompt: A molecule with a permanent dipole sits next to another molecule and causes a dipole to appear in it. Which part of the van der Waals force is at work?

options.label: The Keesom force, between two permanent dipoles
London dispersion, between instantaneous multipoles
The Debye force, between a permanent and an induced multipole
Pauli repulsion, which keeps atoms from close contact

items.explain: Induction is the attraction between a permanent multipole on one molecule and an induced multipole on another, sometimes called the Debye force.

items.prompt: Molecules in a gas or liquid tumble around in thermal motion. Which part of the van der Waals force does this tumbling mostly average out?

options.label: The electrostatic part, which can attract or repel by orientation
The dispersion part, which only attracts
The induction part, which always attracts
None of them; motion affects all parts equally

items.explain: The electrostatic force changes sign on rotation, so thermal motion averages it out to a large extent; induction and dispersion are always attractive and much less affected.
